tool.name: Vue
tool.tagline: Progressive JavaScript framework with fine-grained reactivity and single-file components
tool.description: Vue is a JavaScript framework for building user interfaces from components whose templates update automatically when reactive state changes. It scales from a sprinkle of interactivity on a page to full single-page apps with Vue Router and Pinia, and to server-rendered sites with Nuxt. Vue 3 centres on the Composition API, `<script setup>` single-file components and a Proxy-based reactivity system.

concepts.name: Creating a Vue app
concepts.summary: Scaffold a Vite-powered Vue project, understand single-file components and mount the root component.
concepts.why: Every Vue project starts the same way, and knowing what each generated file does makes the rest of the tooling unsurprising.
concepts.body:
Vue is a **progressive** framework: you can drop it into one page, but most projects are single-page apps built with Vite. Scaffold one with `npm create vue@latest`; it asks about TypeScript, Vue Router, Pinia and testing, then generates a project you run with `npm install` and `npm run dev`.

The building block is the **single-file component** (SFC), a `.vue` file with up to three blocks:

- `<script setup>` — the component's logic, written with the Composition API. Every top-level variable, function and import is usable in the template.
- `<template>` — HTML-like markup with Vue's bindings and directives.
- `<style scoped>` — CSS that applies only to this component's elements.

The entry file `main.js` creates the application and mounts the root component into an element in `index.html`:

```js
createApp(App).mount('#app')
```

`createApp` returns an **app instance** where you register app-wide things before mounting: plugins (`app.use(router)`), global components and `app.config.errorHandler`. Vite compiles each SFC into plain JavaScript: the template becomes an optimised render function, so there is no template parsing in the browser.

Install the official Vue browser devtools early; they show the component tree, state and events, and save hours of `console.log` debugging.
takeaways: `npm create vue@latest` scaffolds a Vite + Vue project
An SFC has `<script setup>`, `<template>` and `<style scoped>` blocks
`createApp(App).mount('#app')` boots the app; register plugins before mounting
pitfalls: Calling `app.use(...)` after `mount()`; plugins must be installed before the app mounts.

quiz.q: In a `<script setup>` block, which variables can the template use?
options: Only those listed in a `return` statement
quiz.explain: `<script setup>` exposes all top-level bindings (variables, functions, imports) to the template automatically.

concepts.name: Template syntax and v-bind
concepts.summary: Render data with mustache interpolation, bind attributes with v-bind (:), and understand what a directive is.
concepts.why: Templates are where most Vue code lives; reading and writing bindings fluently is the first real Vue skill.
concepts.body:
A Vue template is valid HTML extended with bindings. Text interpolation uses double curly braces: `{{ user.name }}` renders the value as text (HTML is escaped, so it is safe against injection).

Inside `{{ }}` and directive values you write **JavaScript expressions**, not statements: `{{ price * qty }}`, `{{ ok ? 'Yes' : 'No' }}` and `{{ formatDate(d) }}` work; `if` blocks and variable declarations do not.

Attributes are not interpolated. To bind one to data, use the **`v-bind`** directive, almost always with its `:` shorthand:

- `:src="avatarUrl"`, `:disabled="isSaving"` — a `false`, `null` or `undefined` boolean value removes the attribute.
- `:id` alone (same-name shorthand, Vue 3.4+) means `:id="id"`.
- `v-bind="attrsObject"` spreads an object of attributes.
- `:[attrName]="value"` binds a dynamic attribute name.

`:class` and `:style` are special: they accept objects and arrays, so `:class="{ active: isActive, 'text-danger': hasError }"` toggles classes and merges with a static `class` attribute.

A **directive** is an attribute starting with `v-` whose value is an expression that Vue re-evaluates whenever its reactive dependencies change. You will meet `v-if`, `v-for`, `v-on` and `v-model` next. `v-html` renders raw HTML: use it only with content you trust.
takeaways: `{{ expr }}` renders escaped text; directives take JavaScript expressions
`:attr="expr"` is shorthand for `v-bind:attr`; falsy booleans remove the attribute
`:class` and `:style` accept objects and arrays
pitfalls: Writing `src="{{ url }}"`; attributes need `:src="url"`, mustaches only work in text.

quiz.q: Which binding correctly sets an image's src from the `url` variable?
quiz.explain: Attributes are bound with v-bind, written `:src`; mustache syntax only works in text content.

concepts.name: Reactive state: ref and reactive
concepts.summary: Declare state with ref() and reactive(), know when .value is needed and why destructuring can break reactivity.
concepts.why: Reactive state is what makes the UI update itself; misunderstanding ref vs reactive causes most beginner bugs.
concepts.body:
Vue re-renders a component when reactive state it used changes. You create that state with two functions.

**`ref(value)`** wraps any value (number, string, object, array) in an object with a `.value` property. In `<script>` you read and write `count.value`; in the template refs are **unwrapped** automatically, so you write `{{ count }}`. Objects inside a ref are made deeply reactive too, so `todos.value.push(x)` triggers updates.

**`reactive(object)`** returns a Proxy of the object itself, with no `.value`: `state.count++`. It has limits:

- It only works with objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, not primitives.
- You cannot replace the whole object (`state = reactive({...})` disconnects the template from the old one).
- Destructuring (`const { count } = state`) copies plain values and loses reactivity; use `toRefs(state)` if you need that.

Because of these limits the Vue docs recommend **`ref` as the default** way to declare state, and many teams use `ref` exclusively.

Updates are **batched**: changing state does not re-render synchronously. Vue queues one update per component per tick. If you need the updated DOM right after a change, `await nextTick()`.

A ref nested in a reactive object is unwrapped on access, but refs inside arrays and Maps are not.
concepts.code:
import { ref, reactive, toRefs, nextTick } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
count.value++
console.log(count.value)            // 1

const todos = ref([])
todos.value.push({ text: 'learn Vue' })   // deep: this is reactive too

const state = reactive({ user: 'Ada', visits: 1 })
state.visits++                      // no .value with reactive

const { visits } = state            // plain number, NOT reactive
const { user } = toRefs(state)      // user is a ref linked to state.user
state.user = 'Grace'
console.log(visits, user.value)     // 2 'Grace'

const box = reactive({ n: ref(1) })
console.log(box.n)                  // 1 (ref unwrapped inside reactive)

await nextTick()                    // DOM now reflects the changes
takeaways: `ref()` for any value, accessed via `.value` in script, unwrapped in templates
`reactive()` proxies an object; don't reassign or destructure it
Updates are batched; `await nextTick()` to see the new DOM
pitfalls: Forgetting `.value` in script: `if (count > 3)` compares the ref object, not the number.
Destructuring a reactive object or props and expecting the copies to stay reactive.

quiz.q: `const state = reactive({ n: 1 }); let { n } = state; state.n = 5;` What is `n` now?
quiz.explain: Destructuring copies the current primitive value (1); the local variable is not connected to the proxy.

quiz.q: Why do the Vue docs recommend ref() as the primary API?
options: It is faster than reactive in every case
It works with any value type and can be reassigned or passed around without losing reactivity
quiz.explain: reactive() only takes objects and breaks on reassignment or destructuring; ref() avoids both limitations.

concepts.name: Computed properties
concepts.summary: Derive values from reactive state with computed(), which caches the result until a dependency changes.
concepts.why: Derived values belong in computed properties, not in duplicated state or expensive template expressions.
concepts.body:
A **computed** property derives a value from other reactive state:

```js
const remaining = computed(() => todos.value.filter(t => !t.done).length)
```

`computed()` returns a read-only ref, so in script you read `remaining.value` and in the template simply `{{ remaining }}`.

Two properties make computeds better than calling a function in the template:

- **Dependency tracking**: Vue records which reactive values the getter read and recomputes only when one of them changes.
- **Caching**: reading it repeatedly returns the cached value; a method would re-run on every render.

Keep getters **pure**: no fetching, no mutating other state, no DOM access. Side effects belong in watchers. Also never mutate the computed result (for example sorting it in place); treat it as a snapshot.

For the rare two-way case, pass `get` and `set` to make a **writable computed**, for example a `fullName` that splits back into first and last names.

Since Vue 3.4 a computed only notifies dependents when its value actually changes, so `const isEven = computed(() => n.value % 2 === 0)` does not re-render consumers when `n` goes from 2 to 4.

A common smell is copying derived data into a `ref` and keeping it in sync with a watcher. If a value can be computed from existing state, make it a computed.
takeaways: `computed(() => ...)` returns a cached, read-only ref
It recomputes only when a reactive dependency changes
Keep getters pure; use get/set only when two-way derivation is needed
pitfalls: Mutating inside a getter, such as `list.value.sort()`, which changes the source state.

quiz.q: A template shows `{{ total }}` three times, where total is a computed over a large array. How many times does the getter run per render if nothing changed?
options: Zero; the cached value is reused
quiz.explain: Computeds are cached until a dependency changes, so unchanged state means no re-evaluation.

concepts.name: Conditionals and lists
concepts.summary: Render conditionally with v-if / v-show and render lists with v-for and a stable :key.
concepts.why: Almost every screen shows or hides things and repeats things; getting keys right prevents subtle UI bugs.
concepts.body:
**`v-if`**, `v-else-if` and `v-else` add or remove elements entirely. To toggle a group without a wrapper element, put `v-if` on a `<template>` tag, which renders nothing itself.

**`v-show`** keeps the element and toggles CSS `display`. Prefer it for things toggled very often (cheap to switch); prefer `v-if` when the condition rarely changes or the content is expensive (it is not rendered at all while false).

**`v-for`** repeats an element for each item:

- Arrays: `v-for="(item, index) in items"`.
- Objects: `v-for="(value, key) in obj"`.
- Ranges: `v-for="n in 5"` gives 1 to 5.

Always give list items a **`:key`** with a stable, unique id (`:key="todo.id"`). Vue uses keys to match old and new elements when the list changes. Without them, or with the array index as key, Vue patches elements in place, so state inside items (input text, component state, focus) can end up attached to the wrong row after inserting, removing or sorting.

Don't put `v-if` and `v-for` on the same element. In Vue 3 `v-if` is evaluated first and cannot see the loop variable. Filter in a computed instead, or wrap with `<template v-for>` and put the `v-if` inside.
takeaways: `v-if` adds/removes elements; `v-show` toggles CSS display
`v-for` needs a stable unique `:key`, not the index, for dynamic lists
Filter with a computed instead of combining v-if and v-for
pitfalls: Using the index as key in a list that can be reordered or have items removed.

quiz.q: A list of inputs uses `:key="index"`. You delete the first item. What can go wrong?
options: Typed text can shift to the wrong row because elements are reused by position
Vue throws a duplicate key error
quiz.explain: With index keys, the element at position 0 is reused for what was item 1, so DOM state stays attached to the wrong data.

concepts.name: Event handling
concepts.summary: Listen to DOM events with v-on (@), call handlers with arguments, and use event and key modifiers.
concepts.why: User interaction drives every app; modifiers remove most event boilerplate.
concepts.body:
**`v-on`**, shortened to `@`, attaches a listener: `@click="handler"`. The value can be:

- A **method name**: `@click="save"` calls `save(event)` with the native event.
- An **inline statement**: `@click="count++"` or `@click="remove(item.id)"`. If you also need the event, pass the special `$event` variable: `@click="remove(item.id, $event)"`.

**Event modifiers** handle common chores declaratively:

- `.prevent` calls `preventDefault()`, e.g. `@submit.prevent="onSubmit"` stops the page reload.
- `.stop` stops propagation; `.self` fires only if the event target is the element itself.
- `.once` removes the listener after the first call; `.passive` marks scroll/touch listeners as passive; `.capture` uses the capture phase.

**Key modifiers** filter keyboard events: `@keyup.enter="send"`, `@keydown.esc="close"`, and combinations with system keys like `@keyup.ctrl.enter`. Add `.exact` to require exactly those modifiers. Mouse buttons have `.left`, `.right` and `.middle`.

Handlers are functions declared in `<script setup>`. Keep template statements short; once a handler does more than one thing, move it into a function. Vue removes listeners automatically when the component unmounts, so you never clean up template listeners yourself (only listeners you add manually with `addEventListener`).
takeaways: `@event="method"` or an inline statement; use `$event` for the native event
`.prevent`, `.stop`, `.once`, `.self` replace manual event-object calls
Key modifiers like `@keyup.enter` filter keyboard events
pitfalls: Forgetting `.prevent` on a form's submit so the browser reloads the page.

quiz.q: What does `@submit.prevent="save"` do?
options: Stops the event from bubbling only
Prevents save from being called twice
quiz.explain: The .prevent modifier calls preventDefault (stopping navigation) before invoking the handler.

concepts.name: Form input bindings with v-model
concepts.summary: Keep form inputs and state in sync with v-model on text inputs, checkboxes, radios and selects.
concepts.why: Forms are everywhere, and v-model removes the value-plus-listener boilerplate for each field.
concepts.body:
**`v-model`** creates a two-way binding between a form element and a ref. It is sugar for a value binding plus an event listener, chosen per element type:

- `<input>` and `<textarea>`: binds `value` and listens to `input`.
- Checkbox: binds `checked` (a boolean). Several checkboxes bound to the same **array** collect the `value`s of the checked ones.
- Radio: the ref holds the `value` of the selected radio.
- `<select>`: the ref holds the selected option's value, or an array with `multiple`.

Modifiers adjust the behaviour:

- `.trim` strips whitespace.
- `.number` casts the input to a number (when it parses).
- `.lazy` syncs on `change` instead of every keystroke.

`v-model` ignores any initial `value`, `checked` or `selected` attributes in the template: the JavaScript state is the single **source of truth**, so set initial values in the ref.

Option values do not have to be strings: bind `:value="obj"` on options or checkboxes and the model receives the object itself.

For validation, keep it simple at first: a computed `errors` object derived from the fields, and a submit handler that checks it. Larger forms usually adopt a library such as VeeValidate or FormKit. You will later learn to make your own components work with `v-model` too.
takeaways: `v-model` = value binding + input listener, adapted to each input type
Several checkboxes on one array ref collect the checked values
`.trim`, `.number` and `.lazy` modify the binding; initial values live in the ref
pitfalls: Setting `value="..."` or `checked` in the template and expecting it to be the initial state; v-model ignores it.

quiz.q: Three checkboxes with values 'a', 'b', 'c' all use v-model="picked" where picked = ref([]). The user checks a and c. What is picked.value?
quiz.explain: When bound to an array, checkboxes add and remove their value in that array.

concepts.name: Components and props
concepts.summary: Split the UI into components, import and use them, and pass data down with defineProps.
concepts.why: Components are Vue's unit of reuse and organisation; props are how parents configure them.
concepts.body:
Each `.vue` file is a component. To use one, import it in `<script setup>` and write it as a tag, conventionally in PascalCase: `<TodoItem />`. No registration step is needed.

A component declares the data it accepts from its parent with **props**, using the `defineProps` compiler macro (no import needed):

```js
const props = defineProps({
  title: { type: String, required: true },
  count: { type: Number, default: 0 },
})
```

With TypeScript you can write `defineProps<{ title: string; count?: number }>()` instead. Since Vue 3.5, destructuring props is reactive and is the idiomatic way to give defaults: `const { title, count = 0 } = defineProps(...)`. The compiler rewrites `count` to `props.count`, so it stays reactive.

The parent passes props as attributes: static `title="Inbox"` or bound `:count="unread"` (without the colon, `count="3"` is the string "3"). Props declared in camelCase can be written kebab-case in templates (`:max-items`).

Props follow **one-way data flow**: when the parent's value changes the child updates, but the child must never assign to a prop. Vue warns if you try. If the child needs a local, editable copy, initialise a ref from the prop; if it wants to change the parent's data, it emits an event (next lesson).
takeaways: Import a component in `<script setup>` and use it as a PascalCase tag
`defineProps` declares inputs; destructure with defaults in Vue 3.5+
Data flows down one way: never assign to a prop
pitfalls: Passing `count="3"` without the colon, which sends the string "3" rather than a number.

quiz.q: A child component wants to change a value it received as a prop from its parent. What is the correct approach?
options: Make the prop a reactive() object and mutate its fields
Emit an event so the parent updates its own state
Use v-if to re-create the parent
quiz.explain: Props are read-only in the child; the owner of the data (the parent) changes it in response to an event.

concepts.name: Component events with defineEmits
concepts.summary: Let children notify parents by declaring and emitting custom events.
concepts.why: Events are the other half of the component contract: props go down, events go up.
concepts.body:
A child talks back to its parent by **emitting events**. Declare them with the `defineEmits` macro, which returns an `emit` function:

```js
const emit = defineEmits(['remove', 'rename'])
emit('rename', newName)
```

The parent listens exactly like a DOM event: `<TodoItem @remove="deleteTodo(todo.id)" @rename="(name) => todo.name = name" />`. Extra arguments passed to `emit` become the handler's arguments. Events emitted in camelCase (`emit('itemSelected')`) can be listened to as `@item-selected`.

In the template you can emit directly with `$emit('remove')`.

With TypeScript, type the payloads with the named-tuple syntax:

```ts
const emit = defineEmits<{ rename: [name: string]; remove: [] }>()
```

Declaring events is not just documentation. Listeners for **undeclared** events fall through to the component's root element as native listeners (see attribute fallthrough), which can make a `click` fire twice. Declared events are also validated in dev and show up in devtools.

Component events **do not bubble**: only the direct parent can listen. For distant communication use provide/inject or a store instead of passing events up through many layers.

A useful convention: name events after what happened (`select`, `close`, `update:modelValue`), not after what the parent should do.
takeaways: `const emit = defineEmits([...])`, then `emit('name', payload)`
Parents listen with `@name`; payload arguments go to the handler
Component events don't bubble; declare all emitted events
pitfalls: Emitting an undeclared `click` event while the root element also fires a native click, so the parent handler runs twice.

quiz.q: A grandchild emits 'save'. Can the grandparent listen with @save on the parent component?
options: No, only the direct parent receives component events
Only if the event name is kebab-case
Yes, component events bubble like DOM events
quiz.explain: Vue component events do not bubble; the middle component would need to re-emit or you use provide/inject or a store.

concepts.name: v-model on components (defineModel)
concepts.summary: Make your own components work with v-model using defineModel, including named and multiple models.
concepts.why: Reusable inputs, toggles and pickers should feel like native inputs to the parent.
concepts.body:
On a component, `v-model="query"` expands to a prop plus an event: `:modelValue="query"` and `@update:modelValue="v => query = v"`. Since Vue 3.4 the **`defineModel()`** macro implements both sides for you:

```js
const model = defineModel()          // a ref synced with the parent
model.value = 'new'                  // emits update:modelValue
```

The returned ref reads the parent's prop and, when you assign to it, emits the update event. You can bind it straight to a native input: `<input v-model="model">`.

Options mirror props: `defineModel({ type: Number, default: 0, required: true })`, or typed with `defineModel<number>()`.

Components can expose **several models** by name. The parent writes `v-model:title="t"` and `v-model:done="d"`, and the child declares `defineModel('title')` and `defineModel('done')`.

Custom **modifiers** are supported: the parent writes `v-model.capitalize="text"` and the child destructures `const [model, modifiers] = defineModel({ set(v) { return modifiers.capitalize ? cap(v) : v } })`.

One subtlety: if the parent does not pass a value, `defineModel` keeps a local value so the component still works uncontrolled. If you give a `default` and the parent passes nothing, the parent's ref and the child can get out of sync, so prefer requiring the model or matching defaults on both sides.
takeaways: `v-model` on a component = `modelValue` prop + `update:modelValue` event
`defineModel()` returns a ref that emits updates when assigned
Use named models (`v-model:title`) for several bindings on one component
pitfalls: Mutating the parent's object via `model.value.field = x`; that bypasses the update event. Assign a new object instead.

quiz.q: Inside a child, `const m = defineModel()` and the code runs `m.value = 5`. What happens?
options: Only the child's local copy changes
Vue warns that props are read-only
The child emits update:modelValue with 5 and the parent's bound ref becomes 5
quiz.explain: defineModel's ref emits the update event on assignment; the parent's v-model listener writes the value.

concepts.name: Slots and scoped slots
concepts.summary: Pass template content into components with default, named and scoped slots.
concepts.why: Slots let one component control layout or behaviour while the parent controls the markup: the basis of layouts, cards, tables and lists.
concepts.body:
Props pass data; **slots** pass template content. A component marks where content goes with `<slot />`; whatever the parent writes between the component's tags is rendered there. Content inside `<slot>` itself is the **fallback** shown when the parent passes nothing.

**Named slots** allow several insertion points. The child writes `<slot name="header" />` and the parent targets it with `<template #header>...</template>` (`#` is short for `v-slot:`). Content outside any `<template #...>` goes to the default slot.

Slot content is compiled in the **parent's scope**: it sees the parent's variables, not the child's. When the child needs to give data to the slot, use a **scoped slot**: the child binds props on the slot, `<slot name="item" :item="row" :index="i" />`, and the parent receives them, typically destructured: `<template #item="{ item, index }">`.

Scoped slots enable **renderless** or headless components: the child owns the logic (fetching, pagination, selection) and the parent decides exactly how each piece looks.

Inside the child, `useSlots()` (or `$slots` in the template) tells you which slots were provided, which is handy for omitting a wrapper: `<header v-if="$slots.header">`. With TypeScript, `defineSlots<{ item(props: { item: Row }): any }>()` types the slot props.
takeaways: `<slot />` renders the parent's content; inner content is the fallback
Named slots: `<slot name="x">` in the child, `<template #x>` in the parent
Scoped slots pass child data up: `<template #item="{ item }">`
pitfalls: Expecting slot content to read the child's variables; it only sees the parent's scope unless passed as slot props.

quiz.q: A child renders `<slot :user="currentUser" />`. How does the parent read currentUser in its default slot content?
options: With `<template #default="{ user }">` (or v-slot on the component)
quiz.explain: Slot props are received through v-slot (# shorthand) and can be destructured.

concepts.name: Watchers and side effects
concepts.summary: Run side effects when state changes with watch and watchEffect, and clean up stale async work.
concepts.why: Fetching on input changes, syncing to localStorage and talking to non-Vue code all need watchers.
concepts.body:
Computeds derive values; **watchers** run side effects in response to changes.

**`watch(source, callback, options)`** watches an explicit source: a ref, a reactive object, a getter function, or an array of these. The callback receives `(newValue, oldValue, onCleanup)`.

- To watch a property of a reactive object or a destructured prop, pass a getter: `watch(() => props.id, ...)` or `watch(() => id, ...)`. Passing `state.count` directly passes a plain number and does not work.
- `{ immediate: true }` runs the callback once right away; `{ once: true }` runs it only on the first change.
- Watching a reactive object is deep automatically; for a ref holding an object, add `{ deep: true }` (or a number to limit depth).

**`watchEffect(fn)`** runs immediately and re-runs whenever any reactive value it read changes, with no explicit source list. It is concise, but its dependencies are implicit and only those read synchronously are tracked.

Async watchers must handle **stale results**: if the id changes twice quickly, the first request may finish last. Vue 3.5 adds `onWatcherCleanup(fn)`, called before the next run and on stop; use it to abort the old request.

By default callbacks run before the component updates; use `{ flush: 'post' }` (or `watchPostEffect`) to see the updated DOM. Watchers created synchronously in `setup` stop with the component; both functions return a stop handle for manual control.
takeaways: `watch(source, cb)` for explicit sources; use a getter for reactive properties and props
`watchEffect` tracks whatever it reads synchronously and runs immediately
Abort stale async work with `onWatcherCleanup` (3.5+) or the onCleanup argument
pitfalls: `watch(state.count, ...)` passes a number, not a source; use `watch(() => state.count, ...)`.
Using a watcher to copy derived data into another ref instead of a computed.

quiz.q: Which correctly watches the `id` prop destructured with `const { id } = defineProps(...)`?
quiz.explain: A destructured prop is compiled to props.id, a property access, so it must be wrapped in a getter to be watched.

concepts.name: Lifecycle hooks and template refs
concepts.summary: Run code when a component mounts or unmounts and get direct access to DOM elements with useTemplateRef.
concepts.why: Integrating charts, maps, focus management and third-party widgets needs the DOM element and the right moment.
concepts.body:
Each component goes through a **lifecycle**: setup runs, the component is mounted into the DOM, it updates when state changes, and finally it unmounts. Register callbacks with:

- `onMounted(fn)` — the DOM exists; initialise third-party libraries, measure elements, add global listeners.
- `onUpdated(fn)` — after a re-render caused by state change (rarely needed).
- `onUnmounted(fn)` — clean up: remove listeners, clear timers, destroy library instances.
- `onBeforeMount`, `onBeforeUpdate`, `onBeforeUnmount` and `onErrorCaptured` exist for finer control.

These must be called **synchronously during setup**, not inside a `setTimeout` or after an `await`, because Vue binds them to the component currently being set up.

During SSR only setup runs; mounted hooks run on the client, so browser-only code belongs in `onMounted`.

To reach a DOM element, add a `ref` attribute in the template and read it with **`useTemplateRef`** (Vue 3.5+):

```js
const input = useTemplateRef('search')   // <input ref="search">
onMounted(() => input.value.focus())
```

The ref is `null` until mount and after unmount. On a component tag, the ref gives the component instance, but with `<script setup>` only what the child exposes via `defineExpose({ ... })` is accessible. Use refs sparingly: most things should be done declaratively through state.
takeaways: `onMounted` for DOM work; `onUnmounted` to clean up
Register hooks synchronously in setup, never after an await
`useTemplateRef('name')` + `ref="name"` gives the element; null before mount
pitfalls: Reading a template ref at the top of `<script setup>`; the element doesn't exist until mounted.

quiz.q: Why might `onMounted` registered after `await fetchConfig()` in setup never run?
options: Lifecycle hooks must be registered synchronously while setup is running
await is not allowed in script setup
quiz.explain: After an await, Vue no longer knows which component is being set up, so the hook can't be bound to it.

concepts.name: Composables
concepts.summary: Extract and reuse stateful logic in useXxx() functions built from refs, computeds, watchers and lifecycle hooks.
concepts.why: Composables are the main reuse mechanism of the Composition API, replacing mixins.
concepts.body:
A **composable** is a function that uses Vue's Composition API to encapsulate stateful logic, named `useSomething` by convention. It can create refs, computeds and watchers and register lifecycle hooks, which then belong to the component that called it.

```js
export function useMouse() {
  const x = ref(0), y = ref(0)
  const update = (e) => { x.value = e.pageX; y.value = e.pageY }
  onMounted(() => window.addEventListener('mousemove', update))
  onUnmounted(() => window.removeEventListener('mousemove', update))
  return { x, y }
}
```

Conventions that make composables pleasant to use:

- **Return a plain object of refs**, not a `reactive()`: callers can destructure (`const { x, y } = useMouse()`) without losing reactivity.
- **Accept refs, getters or plain values** as arguments and normalise them with `toValue()`. Read them inside a `watchEffect` or a watched getter so the composable reacts when the input changes.
- Call composables **synchronously in setup** (like lifecycle hooks), so their hooks attach to the right component.
- Clean up what you set up (listeners, intervals, subscriptions).

Each call creates **independent state**. If you want state shared between components, create it outside the function (module scope) or use a store such as Pinia.

Before writing one, check **VueUse**, a large collection of ready-made composables (`useLocalStorage`, `useFetch`, `useIntersectionObserver` and many more).
takeaways: A composable is a `useX()` function that packages refs, computeds, watchers and hooks
Return an object of refs; accept refs/getters and read them with `toValue()`
Each call has its own state; module-level state or Pinia shares it
pitfalls: Returning `reactive({ x, y })` so callers lose reactivity when they destructure.

quiz.q: Two components each call `useCounter()`, which creates `const count = ref(0)` inside the function. Clicking + in one component...
options: Throws because the ref is shared
quiz.explain: Each call runs the function again and creates a separate ref; sharing needs module-level state or a store.

concepts.name: Provide / inject
concepts.summary: Pass data from an ancestor to any descendant without threading props through every level.
concepts.why: Themes, current user, form context and component libraries rely on provide/inject to avoid prop drilling.
concepts.body:
Passing a prop through five components that don't use it (**prop drilling**) is tedious. With **provide/inject**, an ancestor provides a value under a key and any descendant, however deep, injects it.

```js
// Ancestor
provide('theme', theme)          // theme is a ref
// Descendant
const theme = inject('theme', ref('light'))   // second arg = default
```

Key points:

- Provide **refs** (or reactive objects), not `.value`, so descendants see updates.
- Keep mutations with the provider: provide a read-only view with `readonly(theme)` plus a function like `setTheme`, so it is clear who changes the data.
- The nearest provider wins, so a subtree can override a value.
- `inject` without a default returns `undefined` (and warns) when no ancestor provides the key.
- `app.provide(key, value)` provides to the whole application; plugins use this.

For large apps, use **Symbol keys** to avoid collisions, and with TypeScript type them as `InjectionKey<T>`: `export const ThemeKey: InjectionKey<Ref<string>> = Symbol('theme')`. Put keys in a shared module.

Provide/inject suits **component-tree-scoped** context: a form providing validation state to its fields, a tabs component to its panels, a design system's theme. For global application state (cart, session) a store like Pinia is usually clearer and has devtools support.
takeaways: `provide(key, value)` in an ancestor, `inject(key, default)` in any descendant
Provide refs plus updater functions; wrap in `readonly` to keep mutations in one place
Use Symbol / `InjectionKey` keys in a shared module
pitfalls: Providing `count.value` instead of `count`, so descendants receive a frozen snapshot.

quiz.q: A layout provides 'theme' and a nested section also provides 'theme'. What does a component inside the section inject?
quiz.explain: inject resolves the nearest ancestor that provides the key, so subtrees can override values.

concepts.name: Routing with Vue Router
concepts.summary: Map URLs to components with Vue Router: routes, RouterView, RouterLink, params, lazy loading and guards.
concepts.why: Any multi-page single-page app needs client-side routing, and Vue Router is the official solution.
concepts.body:
**Vue Router** maps URL paths to components. You create a router with a history mode and a route table, install it with `app.use(router)`, and render the matched component with `<RouterView />`:

```js
const router = createRouter({
  history: createWebHistory(),
  routes: [
    { path: '/', component: Home },
    { path: '/users/:id', name: 'user', component: () => import('./UserPage.vue') },
  ],
})
```

- `createWebHistory()` gives clean URLs (the server must serve `index.html` for unknown paths); `createWebHashHistory()` uses `#/` URLs and needs no server config.
- `() => import(...)` **lazy-loads** a route's component as a separate chunk.
- **Dynamic segments** like `:id` appear in `useRoute().params.id`. The same component instance is reused when only params change, so watch `() => route.params.id` to reload data.
- **Nested routes** use `children` plus a `<RouterView />` inside the parent component.

Navigate declaratively with `<RouterLink :to="{ name: 'user', params: { id: 7 } }">` (it adds active classes) or programmatically with `useRouter().push('/')`.

**Navigation guards** control access: `router.beforeEach((to) => { if (to.meta.requiresAuth && !isLoggedIn()) return { name: 'login' } })`. Return `false` to cancel, a route to redirect, or nothing to continue. Per-component hooks like `onBeforeRouteLeave` help with "unsaved changes" prompts.
takeaways: Define routes, `app.use(router)`, render with `<RouterView>`
Lazy-load route components with `() => import(...)`
Params are in `useRoute().params`; watch them when the same component is reused
Guards return false, a redirect route, or nothing
pitfalls: Fetching data only in `onMounted` of a route component; navigating /users/1 to /users/2 reuses the instance and shows stale data.

quiz.q: Navigating from /users/1 to /users/2 with the same route component. What happens by default?
options: Nothing; the URL updates but params stay '1'
The component is destroyed and re-created
The same instance is reused; route.params.id changes
quiz.explain: Vue Router reuses the component when only params change, so code must react to route.params changes.

concepts.name: State management with Pinia
concepts.summary: Share application state across components with Pinia stores: state, getters, actions and storeToRefs.
concepts.why: Pinia is Vue's official store, used for anything many unrelated components need: session, cart, settings, caches.
concepts.body:
When unrelated components need the same state, a **store** gives it one home. **Pinia** is the official choice. Install it with `app.use(createPinia())` and define stores with `defineStore`.

The **setup store** syntax will feel familiar because it is a composable:

```js
export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  const items = ref([])                         // state
  const total = computed(() => ...)             // getter
  function add(product) { items.value.push(product) }   // action
  return { items, total, add }
})
```

Every ref you return becomes state, computeds become getters and functions become actions. You must return all state for devtools and SSR to see it. (An "options store" with `state`, `getters` and `actions` keys also exists.)

In a component, call `const cart = useCartStore()`. The store is a reactive object, so access `cart.items` and `cart.total` without `.value`. All components share the same instance.

Destructuring a store loses reactivity. Use **`storeToRefs(cart)`** for state and getters; actions can be destructured directly.

Benefits over a hand-rolled module-level `ref`: devtools timeline and time travel, SSR safety (one store per request), hot module replacement, `$reset`/`$patch`/`$subscribe` helpers and plugins such as persisted state.

Keep stores focused (one per domain: `useAuthStore`, `useCartStore`) and put async calls in actions.
takeaways: `defineStore('id', () => { ... return {...} })` defines a setup store
Returned refs = state, computeds = getters, functions = actions; return all state
Use `storeToRefs` when destructuring state and getters
pitfalls: `const { total } = useCartStore()` gives a value that never updates; use storeToRefs.

quiz.q: Why use Pinia instead of exporting a module-level ref for shared state in an SSR app?
options: A module-level ref is shared across all server requests, leaking state between users; Pinia creates per-request stores
Module refs don't work with script setup
quiz.explain: On the server a module is evaluated once for all requests, so module-level state is shared across users; Pinia scopes stores to the app instance.

concepts.name: Vue with TypeScript
concepts.summary: Type props, emits, models, refs, template refs, provide/inject and generic components, and check templates with vue-tsc.
concepts.why: Most production Vue code is TypeScript; knowing the typed APIs prevents a lot of runtime bugs.
concepts.body:
Vue 3 is written in TypeScript and `<script setup lang="ts">` gives first-class typing. Type checking of templates is done by **`vue-tsc`** (run in CI with `vue-tsc --noEmit`) and the Vue language tools in your editor.

The main typed APIs:

- **Props**: `defineProps<{ title: string; size?: 'sm' | 'lg' }>()`. With 3.5 destructuring, defaults are plain JavaScript: `const { size = 'sm' } = defineProps<...>()`.
- **Emits**: `defineEmits<{ select: [id: number]; close: [] }>()` types each event's arguments.
- **Models**: `defineModel<string>()` or `defineModel<number>({ required: true })`.
- **Refs**: inference usually works; annotate when the initial value is narrower than later values: `ref<User | null>(null)`.
- **Template refs**: `useTemplateRef<HTMLInputElement>('input')`; recent tooling infers it from the template automatically.
- **Provide/inject**: `InjectionKey<T>` keys make `inject` return `T | undefined`.

**Generic components** take a type parameter on the script tag: `<script setup lang="ts" generic="T extends { id: string }">`. Then `defineProps<{ items: T[] }>()` and slot or emit types can reference `T`, and the parent's usage is checked against the inferred `T`.

Type-only imports in `defineProps` work for interfaces from other files. Keep prop types simple object shapes; the compiler needs to analyse them to generate runtime prop definitions.
concepts.code:
<script setup lang="ts" generic="T extends { id: number }">
import { ref, computed, useTemplateRef, onMounted } from 'vue'

const { items, max = 10 } = defineProps<{ items: T[]; max?: number }>()
const emit = defineEmits<{ select: [item: T]; clear: [] }>()
const query = defineModel<string>('query', { default: '' })

const selected = ref<T | null>(null)
const shown = computed(() => items.slice(0, max))
const search = useTemplateRef<HTMLInputElement>('search')
onMounted(() => search.value?.focus())

function pick(item: T) {
  selected.value = item
  emit('select', item)        // emit('select', 42) would be a type error
}
</script>

<template>
  <input ref="search" v-model="query">
  <slot v-for="item in shown" :key="item.id" :item="item" :pick="pick" />
</template>
takeaways: `defineProps<T>()`, `defineEmits<{ e: [args] }>()`, `defineModel<T>()`
Annotate refs whose type widens: `ref<User | null>(null)`
`generic="T"` on the script tag creates generic components
Run `vue-tsc --noEmit` to type-check templates
pitfalls: Relying on `tsc` alone; it ignores `.vue` files and templates, so use `vue-tsc`.

quiz.q: Which command type-checks .vue files including their templates?
quiz.explain: Plain tsc doesn't understand SFCs; vue-tsc wraps it with Vue's language tooling.

concepts.name: Transition, Teleport and KeepAlive
concepts.summary: Animate entering and leaving elements, render modals outside the component tree and cache inactive components.
concepts.why: These built-ins solve common UI problems (animations, modals, preserving tab state) that are tricky to hand-roll.
concepts.body:
Vue ships several built-in components.

**`<Transition>`** animates a single element or component that is inserted or removed by `v-if`, `v-show`, a dynamic component or a key change. It adds classes at the right moments: with `name="fade"` you style `fade-enter-from`, `fade-enter-active`, `fade-leave-to` and `fade-leave-active`. `mode="out-in"` waits for the old element to leave before the new one enters. JavaScript hooks (`@enter`, `@leave`) let you use an animation library. **`<TransitionGroup>`** animates items in a `v-for` list, including moves via the `*-move` class; items need keys.

**`<Teleport to="body">`** renders its content elsewhere in the DOM while keeping it logically inside the component (props, events and provide/inject still work). Use it for modals, toasts and tooltips that must escape `overflow: hidden` or z-index stacking. `:disabled` keeps the content in place, and Vue 3.5's `defer` prop lets the target be rendered later in the same tick.

**`<KeepAlive>`** caches component instances instead of destroying them when they are switched out, typically around `<component :is="tab">` or `<RouterView>`'s slot. State and scroll positions survive tab switches. Limit it with `include`, `exclude` and `max`. Cached components get `onActivated` and `onDeactivated` hooks instead of mount/unmount on each switch.

**`<Suspense>`** coordinates async components and async setup; it is still marked experimental.
takeaways: `<Transition name="x">` adds x-enter-from / x-leave-to etc. classes around v-if/v-show
`<Teleport to="body">` moves DOM output but keeps component relationships
`<KeepAlive>` caches switched-out components; use `onActivated`/`onDeactivated`
pitfalls: Wrapping several root elements in `<Transition>`; it animates one element, use `<TransitionGroup>` for lists.

quiz.q: A modal inside a card with overflow: hidden gets clipped. Which built-in fixes it while keeping the modal's props and events working?
quiz.explain: Teleport renders the modal's DOM under another target (like body) while it stays a child in the component tree.

concepts.name: Advanced reactivity APIs
concepts.summary: Control reactivity precisely with shallowRef, triggerRef, markRaw, toRaw, readonly, customRef and effectScope.
concepts.why: Large data sets, third-party class instances and library code need finer control than ref and reactive give by default.
concepts.body:
Default reactivity is **deep**: every nested object is wrapped in a Proxy on access. That is convenient but has costs for large or foreign data. The advanced APIs give you control.

- **`shallowRef(value)`** tracks only `.value` assignment, not nested changes. Ideal for large immutable data (replace it wholesale: `rows.value = newRows`) and for holding component definitions or class instances. After mutating inside one, call **`triggerRef(r)`** to force an update.
- **`shallowReactive(obj)`** makes only top-level properties reactive.
- **`markRaw(obj)`** flags an object so Vue never proxies it: map instances, chart objects, SDK clients.
- **`toRaw(proxy)`** returns the original object, useful for passing to libraries, `structuredClone`, or comparing identity.
- **`readonly(x)`** gives a deep read-only proxy that warns on mutation.
- **`customRef((track, trigger) => ({ get, set }))`** builds a ref with custom timing, such as a debounced ref.
- **`effectScope()`** groups effects created inside `scope.run(() => ...)` so `scope.stop()` disposes them all at once. It is how libraries create shared state outside components.

Identity gotcha: `reactive(obj) !== obj`. Mutating the raw object bypasses tracking, and storing the raw object in a Set then searching for the proxy fails. Always work through the proxy (or consistently through the raw object with markRaw).
takeaways: `shallowRef` + replacement for large or external data; `triggerRef` after in-place edits
`markRaw` keeps class instances and library objects out of the proxy system
`effectScope` collects effects so they can be stopped together
pitfalls: Comparing a reactive proxy with the raw object by identity (`===`), or mixing both in Sets and Maps.

quiz.q: You store a 3D-engine scene object in a ref and the app becomes slow. What is the most likely fix?
options: Wrap it with markRaw() or hold it in a shallowRef
quiz.explain: Deep reactivity proxies every nested property of the huge object; markRaw or shallowRef avoids that.

concepts.name: Custom directives and plugins
concepts.summary: Encapsulate low-level DOM behaviour in custom directives and package app-wide features as plugins.
concepts.why: Directives and plugins are how you extend Vue itself, and how most Vue libraries are installed.
concepts.body:
Composables reuse stateful logic; **custom directives** reuse low-level DOM manipulation on plain elements. A directive is an object of lifecycle hooks: `created`, `beforeMount`, `mounted`, `beforeUpdate`, `updated`, `beforeUnmount`, `unmounted`. Each receives `(el, binding, vnode)`, where `binding.value` is the expression's value, `binding.arg` is the argument (`v-tooltip:top` gives `'top'`) and `binding.modifiers` is an object of modifiers.

In `<script setup>`, any camelCase variable starting with `v` is usable as a directive: `const vFocus = { mounted: (el) => el.focus() }` enables `<input v-focus>`. A function shorthand runs on both `mounted` and `updated`. Register globally with `app.directive('focus', vFocus)`.

Prefer components or composables when possible; directives are for things like focus, click-outside, intersection observers and tooltips. They do not work well on components with multiple root nodes.

A **plugin** is an object with `install(app, options)` (or just a function). Inside it you can:

- register components and directives with `app.component` / `app.directive`,
- make values available with `app.provide(key, value)`,
- add `app.config.globalProperties.$x` for template access (use sparingly),
- set `app.config.errorHandler` or other app config.

Users install it with `app.use(plugin, options)`. Vue Router, Pinia and i18n libraries are all plugins.
takeaways: Directives are objects of hooks receiving `(el, binding)`; use them for DOM-level behaviour
In script setup, `vSomething` variables are directives automatically
A plugin is `install(app, options)`; it registers components, directives and provides
pitfalls: Forgetting to remove listeners in `unmounted`, leaking handlers for every mounted element.

quiz.q:
What is `binding.arg` for `

`?
quiz.explain: The part after the colon is the argument; modifiers come after dots and the value is the expression.

concepts.name: Performance optimisation
concepts.summary: Find and fix slow Vue apps: lazy loading, stable props, v-once and v-memo, shallow state and list virtualisation.
concepts.why: Vue is fast by default, but large lists, heavy components and careless props can still make apps sluggish.
concepts.body:
Measure first: the Vue devtools performance timeline and the browser profiler show which components render often or slowly. Then apply the matching fix.

**Load less**: lazy-load routes and heavy components with `defineAsyncComponent(() => import('./Chart.vue'))`; check bundle sizes; import only what you use from big libraries.

**Update less**:

- **Props stability**: a child re-renders when any prop it receives changes. Passing `:active-id="activeId"` to every row re-renders all rows on each change; passing `:active="item.id === activeId"` re-renders only the two affected rows.
- **`v-once`** renders a subtree once and skips it forever after.
- **`v-memo="[item.selected]"`** skips updating a subtree (often a `v-for` row) unless the listed values change.
- **Computed stability**: since 3.4 computeds trigger only when their value changes, but returning a new object each time defeats that; compare manually if needed.

**Track less**: deep reactivity over huge arrays costs memory and time. Use `shallowRef` for large data you replace wholesale and `markRaw` for non-UI objects.

**Render less**: lists with thousands of rows should be **virtualised** (render only visible rows) with a library such as vue-virtual-scroller or TanStack Virtual. Avoid needless component abstraction in hot loops; each component instance has overhead.

Production builds strip dev warnings and are much faster than dev mode; always profile production.
takeaways: Profile in production mode before optimising
Keep props stable: pass derived booleans, not shared ids, to list rows
`v-once`, `v-memo`, `shallowRef`, async components and virtualisation cover most hot spots
pitfalls: Using `v-memo` with an incomplete dependency array, so rows don't update when other data changes.

quiz.q: Every row receives :selected-id="selectedId" and compares it internally. Selecting a new row re-renders...
options: Only the old and new selected rows
Every row, because each row's prop changed
quiz.explain: Each row's selectedId prop changes, so all rows update; passing a per-row boolean limits updates to two rows.

concepts.name: How reactivity works inside
concepts.summary: Understand Vue's Proxy-based tracking: track and trigger, effects and subscribers, the scheduler and the 3.5 version-counting redesign.
concepts.why: Knowing the mechanism explains every reactivity gotcha and is essential when writing libraries or debugging edge cases.
concepts.body:
Vue's reactivity is a runtime dependency graph built from **Proxies** and **getter/setter refs**.

`reactive(obj)` returns a Proxy whose `get` trap calls **track** (record that the currently running effect depends on `target.key`) and returns the value, lazily wrapping nested objects in proxies. The `set` and `deleteProperty` traps call **trigger**, which notifies every subscriber of that key. Array methods like `push` and iteration are instrumented specially (iteration tracks an internal key, length changes trigger it). A `ref` is an object whose `value` getter and setter do the same tracking for one value.

An **effect** is a function run while it is the "active subscriber", so every reactive read it performs subscribes it. Component render functions, `computed` and `watch` are all built on this. Dependencies are recollected on every run, which is why branches not taken don't subscribe.

Vue 3.5 rewrote the internals: each dependency keeps a **version** counter and subscribers are linked through doubly linked lists. A computed is lazy and only recomputes if a dependency's version changed since it last ran, which made computeds cheaper and reduced memory use substantially.

Triggered component updates don't run immediately: they are queued as jobs in a **scheduler**, deduplicated, sorted parent-first and flushed in a microtask. `nextTick()` returns that flush's promise. Watchers default to the `pre` flush (before component updates), `post` runs after, and `sync` runs immediately on every change.

Reads outside an effect, through `toRaw`, or after an `await` in an effect are not tracked.
takeaways: Proxy `get` tracks the running effect; `set` triggers subscribers of that key
Renders, computeds and watchers are all effects; dependencies are recollected each run
Component updates are batched by a scheduler and flushed in a microtask (`nextTick`)
3.5 uses per-dependency versions so computeds recompute only when needed
pitfalls: Expecting reads after an `await` inside `watchEffect` to be tracked; only the synchronous part is.

quiz.q: Inside watchEffect, code reads a.value, then awaits a fetch, then reads b.value. Changing b later...
options: Does not re-run it, because b was read after the await when no effect was active
quiz.explain: Tracking only happens while the effect runs synchronously; after the await the active subscriber is gone.

quiz.q: Why does `state.count++` three times in one handler cause only one re-render?
options: Only the last set trap runs
Update jobs are queued, deduplicated and flushed once in a microtask
quiz.explain: Trigger schedules the component's update job; the scheduler dedupes it and runs it once at the next flush.

concepts.name: Compiler, virtual DOM and render functions
concepts.summary: See how templates compile to render functions with patch flags, block trees and cached static content, and when to write render functions yourself.
concepts.why: Understanding compile-time optimisations explains Vue's performance profile and enables render functions for highly dynamic components.
concepts.body:
Vue uses a **virtual DOM**: a render function returns a tree of vnodes, and the runtime **patches** the real DOM by diffing the new tree against the previous one. Vue's twist is a **compiler-informed** virtual DOM: because templates are statically analysable, the compiler emits hints that let the runtime skip most of the diffing.

- **Static hoisting / caching**: fully static elements are created once and reused across renders.
- **Patch flags**: each dynamic vnode carries a bitmask saying what can change (`TEXT`, `CLASS`, `PROPS` with a list of prop names...), so patching checks only those.
- **Block tree**: a block (a template root, or the inside of a `v-if`/`v-for`) collects its dynamic descendants into a flat `dynamicChildren` array. Updates walk that array instead of the whole subtree, so the cost scales with dynamic nodes, not template size.

You can see the output in the Vue SFC Playground's JS tab.

Hand-written **render functions** use `h(type, props, children)`, or JSX via a plugin. Use them for components whose structure is very dynamic (e.g. a heading level from a prop, or components that generate markup from data), and in libraries. They lose compiler optimisations and are harder to read, so templates remain the default. A `<script setup>` component can't return a render function, but `setup()` in `defineComponent` can.

Vue's upcoming **Vapor mode** compiles templates directly to DOM operations without a virtual DOM, for opt-in components.
takeaways: Templates compile to render functions returning vnodes; the runtime patches the DOM
Patch flags, block trees and static caching let updates skip static parts
`h(type, props, children)` render functions suit highly dynamic components
pitfalls: Rewriting ordinary components as render functions for speed; templates are usually faster thanks to compiler hints.

quiz.q: Why does a mostly static 500-line template update quickly when only one text binding changes?
options: The block tree's dynamicChildren lists only the dynamic nodes, and patch flags limit checks to the text
quiz.explain: The compiler records the dynamic nodes and what can change on them, so patching visits only that span's text.

concepts.name: SSR, hydration and Nuxt
concepts.summary: Render Vue on the server, hydrate it in the browser, avoid hydration mismatches and know what Nuxt adds.
concepts.why: Server rendering improves first paint and SEO but introduces state-leak and mismatch bugs that need expert understanding.
concepts.body:
With **server-side rendering**, the server runs your components to produce HTML, the browser shows it immediately, and then Vue **hydrates** it: it creates the same app with `createSSRApp`, walks the existing DOM instead of creating it, and attaches listeners and reactivity.

On the server you call `renderToString(app)` (or a streaming variant) from `vue/server-renderer`. Only `setup` and server-safe code run; `onMounted` and other DOM hooks do not, so browser APIs belong there.

Two classes of bugs dominate:

- **Cross-request state pollution**: modules are evaluated once per server process, so module-level refs or stores are shared by all users. Create the app, router and Pinia **per request**.
- **Hydration mismatches**: if the client's first render differs from the server HTML (dates, `Math.random()`, `window` checks, invalid HTML nesting like a `div` inside a `p`), Vue warns and patches. Fix the cause: render such values only after mount, or mark an intentional difference with Vue 3.5's `data-allow-mismatch` attribute. Use `useId()` for ids that must match on both sides.

Vue 3.5 adds **lazy hydration** for async components: `defineAsyncComponent({ loader, hydrate: hydrateOnVisible() })` delays hydrating below-the-fold parts (also `hydrateOnIdle`, `hydrateOnInteraction`, `hydrateOnMediaQuery`).

Hand-rolled SSR is rare. **Nuxt** provides SSR, static generation, file-based routing, data fetching (`useFetch`, `useAsyncData`) with server-to-client payload transfer, and server routes. Learning raw SSR mainly helps you debug Nuxt.
takeaways: SSR renders HTML on the server; hydration attaches Vue to it with `createSSRApp`
Create app, router and stores per request to avoid leaking state between users
Mismatches come from non-deterministic or browser-only render output; fix or mark them
Nuxt packages SSR, routing and data fetching for real projects
pitfalls: Rendering `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()` during SSR; the client renders a different time and hydration mismatches.

quiz.q: A store defined as a module-level reactive object is used in an SSR app. What is the risk?
options: The store won't be reactive on the client
None, modules are re-evaluated per request
State from one user's request can leak into another user's render
quiz.explain: Server modules are evaluated once and shared by all requests, so module-level state is shared across users.
